title: I know that I don't know
word: I know that I don't know
hook: the oracle calls Socrates wisest, and he decides it's because he knows he doesn't know (Plato, Apology 21)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Socrates' last day: a whole day of hard questions, welcomed. Your line was keep asking. What real question did you ask? Day eighty-six.

Notice how rarely anyone says it. In a meeting, someone asks a question, and there's a small pause, and then someone answers confidently, and later it turns out they were guessing. Online, everyone has a take on everything within the hour. Even among friends, it can feel like losing to say three little words: I don't know. Today we go back a few years before yesterday's prison, to the reason Socrates became Socrates. It starts with a friend making a trip to the most famous oracle in the Greek world, and asking a very bold question. Today's story is I know that I don't know.
screen: `A PAUSE, THEN A CONFIDENT GUESS.` → `A TAKE ON EVERYTHING.` → `A QUESTION FOR THE ORACLE.`

segments.voice: It's in Plato's Apology, his version of the speech Socrates gave at his trial. Socrates tells the jury that his friend Chaerephon, an excitable man, once went to the oracle of Apollo at Delphi and asked: is anyone wiser than Socrates? And the priestess answered: no one. Socrates says this baffled him. He knew he wasn't wise. But a god doesn't lie. So he set out to test it. He went to a politician with a great reputation for wisdom, and questioned him, and found that the man thought he knew a great deal, and didn't. And Socrates walked away thinking, more or less: well, I'm a little wiser than him in this one small way. Neither of us knows anything very fine and good. But he thinks he knows, and I don't think I know. Then he tried the poets, and found they wrote beautiful things but couldn't explain them. Then the craftsmen, who really did know their crafts, but assumed that made them experts on everything else too. So he concluded the oracle meant something humbling: human wisdom is worth little, and the wisest person is the one who knows it. Here's a surprise. The famous line, I know that I know nothing, isn't in Plato in those words. It's a later summary. What Socrates actually claims is smaller and more precise: I don't think I know what I don't know. And notice what it cost. Going around showing important people what they didn't know made him enemies, and helped lead to that trial. But it also made him the one person in Athens you could learn from. You can't learn anything you already think you know.
screen: `IS ANYONE WISER THAN SOCRATES?` · `POLITICIANS, POETS, CRAFTSMEN.` · `HE THINKS HE KNOWS; I DON'T.` · `NOT QUITE THE FAMOUS LINE.` · then, large: `I DON'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say I don't know once today. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you have a strong opinion about, but haven't looked into much. Just one thing. Notice how sure you feel. Now ask, the way Socrates would: how do I actually know that? What would I need to see to be sure? Let a little space open up where the certainty was. It can feel uncomfortable, even a little free. Rest in that space. The bell holds the time.
I know that I don't know. Socrates' reading of the oracle: the wisest person is the one who doesn't think they know what they don't. Today's word.
screen: `I KNOW THAT I DON'T KNOW — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: I don't know. Today, when you're asked something you're not sure about, say it plainly, and add: let's find out. Day eighty-six.

screen: `DAY 86 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BROTHER LAWRENCE IN THE KITCHEN.`

howItsDone: Teachers of philosophy often start with Socrates' reading of the oracle, and many people in science, law and medicine treat an honest I don't know as the start of careful work.

fork.setup: you're Socrates. the oracle has said no one is wiser than you, and you know you're not wise. what do you do?
options: accept it and start teaching as the wisest man
test it by questioning people thought to be wise
fork.reveal: he tests it: politicians, poets, craftsmen. he decides he's wiser only in this: he doesn't think he knows what he doesn't know.

original.note: Greek: know yourself. a saying inscribed at Apollo's temple at Delphi, where the oracle spoke.

trapdoor: what you thought: a clever line about knowing nothing.
what it means: not thinking you know what you don't is the beginning of real learning.
what a scholar hears: Apology 21–22; the slogan I know that I know nothing is a later paraphrase, not Plato's wording.

notes: Apology 20e–23b paraphrased (Jowett 1871 is public domain but not on the validator's list). Confirm Chaerephon, the Pythia's answer, and the order politicians, poets, craftsmen.
The claim that 'I know that I know nothing' does not appear in Plato in that form is widely held; confirm.
Greek γνῶθι σεαυτόν inscribed at Delphi (per Pausanias and others): confirm.
